newsitem.title: GERMANY: German exporters, shares cheer dollar advance.
newsitem.headline: German exporters, shares cheer dollar advance.

text.p: The dollar hit dizzy heights against the deutschemark on Monday, delighting German exporters and boosting the equity market, despite clear signs the powerful Bundesbank seemed keen to brake the dollar's ascent.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer briefly halted the dollar's grinding advance last Thursday when he said he thought the U.S. unit's rise from its historic lows of 1995 had finished.
But in afternoon trade in Europe the dollar was hovering around 1.79 marks, having earlier hit a six-year high of 1.7960 marks. Tietmeyer's comments had been made at around 1.76 marks.
And foreign exchange market players said the upside had not been reached yet.

"The dollar is still appreciating. The rise... is sound and fundamentally well-backed. We see 1.76 marks as the downside, but wouldn't rule out 1.84 marks being reached," said Folker Hellmeyer, senior forex dealer at Helaba Bank in Frankfurt.

Dealers said that Tietmeyer's use of calming phrases aimed at slowing the dollar's rise were starting to sound like "the boy who cried wolf" and that repeated recourse to this approach has already ultimately failed to impress the market.
"The market has disregarded Tietmeyer for good reason. The more often he uses this tool, the less impact it will have eventually," Hellmeyer said.

The Bundesbank's calls for a weaker dollar are not only running against the market, but also fly in the face of German exporters, who have made clear they are benefiting from their goods selling cheaper abroad.

The export sector is one of the few areas where Germany is registering anything near satisfactory levels of growth. Growth in the domestic market is sluggish, unemployment is at or around post-war levels and consumer spending is muted.

The rise in the dollar has boosted Germany's DAX index by a massive 44 percent since the start of the year. The main engine for DAX growth has been exporting stocks in the chemical sector, including BASF AG, Hoechst AG and Bayer AG.
Car stocks have also reaped the benefits of the weak mark, including Volkswagen AG, Daimler-Benz AG and BMW AG.

Tietmeyer lashed out at the DAX's gains last week by insisting that the index is not a representative gauge for the overall state of the economy, hinting instead at concern about asset inflation and the dangers of a weak currency.
At the same time, he insisted that he did not wish to step into U.S. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's shoes. Greenspan hit markets hard late last year when he criticised their "irrational exuberance".
But with no progress seen on planned reforms to help boost German competitiveness, major companies are seeing the weak mark as a welcome boost to their earnings.
"Our government is not able to get any major structural reforms on their way and this will prevail until next year's elections. The market hasn't yet acknowledged this fact," Hellmeyer said.

Although the Bundesbank has made veiled threats about possible intervention to support the mark -- wary that a weak mark in the run-up to European Monetary Union could mean a weak euro -- such a move is seen as unlikely unless major central banks take concerted action.

"(Intervention) doesn't make any sense. If there is to be an intervention, then we will have a joint action by all the big central banks," Werner Becker, economist at Deutsche Bank Research, who is forecasting a rise to 1.80 marks and slightly above in the next six months.
